title: Identity
instruction: Pick the lockup that fits the surface and size, and give it room on every side.
intro: The wordmark is our name drawn as one piece of artwork: OATH and ACTION in heavy capitals, joined by ampersand B, the red ampersand we drew for Oath & Action. A lockup is a fixed arrangement of the wordmark with another part, such as the tagline or the lockmark, the 3 by 3 grid of nodes that chapter 08 explains.

Every mark here is a vector master drawn for a range of sizes. You place the master, color it with tokens and leave room around it. In this chapter x means the height of the wordmark’s capitals, and the pages show today’s wordmark width. The condensed width, which Dustin Cathcart is weighing, appears only in the wordmark width proofs after chapter 08.

rules.title: Place the wordmark from its master file.
rules.rule: Use the master drawn for the height you need and set its color with tokens. Never type the name in a font, Inter Tight included, though the capitals were cut from it.

why.text: The masters set every gap between letters by eye and give the ampersand the same white on each side, 0.203x, so the name keeps one shape from a 16 px email footer to a printed banner. Ampersand B exists only as drawn artwork. A typed name takes the font’s ampersand and the font’s spacing, and a reader who meets two slightly different names starts to wonder which one is ours.

correct.caption: The display master at 440 px wide on Newsprint, with its construction drawn in: the cap line and baseline, x, one cap height of clear space and the white on each side of the ampersand.

failure.caption: The name typed in Inter Tight 800 for a slide. The font’s own ampersand stands in for B, the gaps come out wide and uneven, and the result no longer matches the masthead the reader saw a minute earlier.

rules.builders: Pick the file by the height you will draw it. Set color to the surface’s primary text token and --amp to its signature token; the file reads both. On Prussian, place the file from prussian/, which carries White in the drawing.

rules.title: Choose the lockup by the space and the surface.
rules.rule: Eight lockups cover every use, and each has one job. Start from the width you have: L1 for most uses, L3 for the site and email masthead, L2 for square formats and posters, L8 where the full name will not fit. The sheet after this rule shows all eight at true size, and the specifications give each one’s minimum.

why.text: A fixed set means a reader meets the same arrangement in the same place, and a producer never has to invent one. Each lockup’s job comes from the space it fills, so the choice turns on two facts you can measure: the width you have and the surface under it.

correct.caption: A 120 px tile in a partner directory carries L8 at 74 px wide, so its capitals stand 25 px tall.

failure.caption: The same tile with the full wordmark squeezed in at 100 px wide. Its capitals drop to 10 px, under the 14 px floor, and the white around the ampersand fills in.

rules.builders: Check the lockup’s minimum before you place it. When the space falls under that minimum, switch to the lockup Rule 03.4’s table names. L4 to L7 have no master files of their own yet: build them from the wordmark, monogram and tagline masters on the layouts from our brand guide’s fifth edition, as the sheet shows, or ask the editor for a file.

rules.title: Keep one cap height of clear space on every side.
rules.rule: Leave 1.0x of open space around the lockup’s outer edge, with its tagline and lockmark inside that edge. Text, rules, image edges and other logos all stay outside it. In a partnership lockup the hairline and the partner’s logo belong to the lockup, so the clear space runs around all three (Rule 03.8). Over a photograph, set the lockup on a solid Newsprint or Charcoal panel with the same space inside the panel.

why.text: Open space lets the eye find the name before it reads anything else, and it keeps a headline or a partner’s logo from reading as part of our mark. A measure of one cap height grows with the mark, so the rule holds at every size.

correct.caption: A page head at true size: L1 at 32 px tall, its clear space drawn in, and the headline set below that space.

failure.caption: The same page head with the headline moved up to 9 px under the wordmark, 0.3x. The headline’s first words read as part of the name.

rules.title: Keep every mark at or above its minimum size.
rules.rule: On screen, no identity mark draws its capitals under 14 px, and no tagline inside a lockup sets under 13 px. In print, no capitals under 3 mm and no tagline under 7 pt. Under a lockup’s minimum, switch to the lockup the table names.

why.text: Each master was drawn and checked at its smallest size, where the wordmark keeps its six enclosed counters, the holes inside letters such as O and A, and the ampersand keeps its two. Our fifth edition scaled one drawing to every size, and at its own 120 px minimum a notch in the ampersand closed into a seventh enclosed shape.

correct.caption: Every mark at its screen minimum, at true size. These are graphics drawn at their smallest allowed size, so the 13 px floor for text does not apply to the letters inside them.

failure.caption: The display master scaled to 12 px tall for an email footer. Its capitals fall to 11 px, the white around the ampersand fills in and the name blurs. The 16 px master, 152 px wide, fits the same footer.

rules.builders: Read the height you will draw, then pick the master whose range holds it: the 16 px master from 16 to 19 px tall, the 24 px master from 20 to 39 px, the display master from 40 px. In print, set the width in inches from the table.

rules.title: Set the marks in their colors on the four approved surfaces.
rules.rule: Newsprint, White and Charcoal carry the wordmark with its red ampersand. On Prussian every mark goes White, ampersand and lever included, because red never sits on Prussian (Rule 05.3). One-color versions in Charcoal or White serve one-color print, embossing and watermarks.

why.text: Each surface has one ink that reads on it: Charcoal on Newsprint at 13.29:1, Newsprint on Charcoal at 13.29:1, White on Prussian at 13.28:1. Pillar Red measures 3.19:1 on Prussian, just over the 3:1 a graphic needs, but once drawn small it falls short: our fifth edition’s red ampersand measured 2.27:1 there at 16 px. Red on our dark blue also reads as a pair of party colors, which Rule 01.1 keeps off every page.
why.basis: Design judgment, measured against WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 at rendered sizes; Rule 05.3 for red

correct.caption: L1, L2 and L8 on six grounds at true size: Newsprint, White and Charcoal with the red ampersand, Prussian in White, and the one-color versions.

failure.caption: The Newsprint file dropped onto a Charcoal slide. The Charcoal letters vanish into the ground and only the red ampersand shows.

rules.title: Use L3 for the masthead, and drop the lockmark when the bar gets narrow.
rules.rule: The masthead is the bar across the top of every page and email. From 48em wide, 768 px at the default text size, it sets L3: the wordmark at left and the lockmark at its right, 2.4 cap heights tall. Under 48em, it sets L1 from the 24 px master beside the menu button. Email takes L3 as an image.

why.text: The masthead is the one place every reader sees the mark, so it carries the fullest lockup the width allows. The lockmark needs about 34 px to show its nine nodes and its lever, and on a phone that room goes to the menu button.

correct.caption: Three mastheads at true size: the site at 1440 px, the site on a 390 px phone and a 600 px email header, each from the master drawn for its height.

failure.caption: L3 squeezed to 150 px across a phone bar. Its capitals fall to 12 px and the lockmark’s nodes and links run together at 28 px.

rules.builders: Write the switch as a media query in em, @media (min-width: 48em), so it follows the reader’s text size (Rule 07.5). In email, export the masthead as a PNG at twice its size with the alt text “Oath & Action”. Most email clients drop web fonts, and several show no inline SVG.

rules.title: Use L8 as the one monogram, and retire the spaced “O & A”.
rules.rule: L8 sets O and A with ampersand B between them, cut from the same masters as the wordmark. It serves small squares where the full name will not fit, from 48 px wide. The compact signature from our brand guide’s fourth edition, “O & A” typed with word spaces, retires, along with any other typed monogram.

why.text: Two monograms split what readers learn to recognize. L8 keeps the wordmark’s own white beside the ampersand, so it reads as the name in brief. Typed with spaces, the three characters read as separate letters, and the font’s ampersand replaces B.

correct.caption: L8 at its 48 px minimum and at 120 px, on Newsprint and on Charcoal.

failure.caption: Our fourth edition’s compact signature, typed in Inter Tight with word spaces and the font’s own ampersand.

rules.title: Join a partner with a hairline, and keep our ampersand inside our name.
rules.rule: In a partnership lockup the host’s name leads: on a piece we host, L1 sits at left; on a piece the partner hosts, the partner’s logo sits at left and L1 follows. A 1 px vertical hairline stands between them with 0.6x of space on each side, and the partner’s logo stands no taller than our capitals. For a square, set L8 beside the partner’s logo the same way. Our ampersand stays inside the wordmark, and a second ampersand or a plus sign never joins the two names.

why.text: The ampersand is our hinge between an oath and the action that keeps it. Used to join two organizations, it turns our mark into a conjunction anyone can borrow, and the reader sees one organization with a long name. A hairline marks a partnership and gives each name its own field, and the host leads because a reader first wants to know who is holding the event.
why.basis: Design judgment; Dustin Cathcart’s ruling on partners, November 6, 2026

correct.caption: Two partnership lockups at true size, each led by the host: our name on a piece we host, the partner’s on a piece it hosts. The partner is invented.

failure.caption: An event flyer that joins the names with a second ampersand, so it reads as one organization called “Oath & Action & Merrimack Valley Civic Lab”.

rules.builders: Ask the partner for its logo file and its own clear-space rule, and give each mark the larger of the two. Place the partner’s logo as the partner draws it, ampersand and all; write “and” for a partner’s ampersand only in copy we type (Rule 01.24). Send the finished piece to the editor before it prints or posts.
